Direct-acting (or “instantaneous”) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the electricity they draw into heat in the room – so at the point of use they are fully efficient. However, when you look at the bigger picture (primary energy and cost), they are generally less favourable than other heating options.  

Key points:  
• On-site efficiency vs. primary energy  
  – 100 % of the electrical energy becomes heat in the radiator.  
  – Electricity generation and transmission typically incurs losses (often a primary-energy factor of 2.5–3.0), so from a system perspective you “use up” more fuel or renewables upstream.  

• Operating cost  
  – Electricity prices per kWh are usually higher than for district heating, natural gas or heat pump output (which may deliver 2–4 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity used).  
  – Direct electric radiators therefore tend to carry a higher running cost in cold climates or for large, continuously heated areas.  

• Appropriate application

Here are several practical tips for getting the most out of direct-acting electric radiators. While actual results will vary with your home’s insulation, occupancy pattern and electricity tariff, these measures often help improve comfort and may reduce running costs:

1. Use built-in thermostats and timers  
   • Program each radiator to come on only when you need it (for example, 15–30 minutes before you wake up or return home).

An energy declaration (in Sweden often called an “energideklaration”) is a standardized energy performance certificate that describes how much energy a building uses and how efficiently it operates. It is carried out by an accredited energy inspector and must be renewed every ten years. Key elements include:

• Legal framework  
  – Governed by the European Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), transposed into Swedish law.  
  – Required when a building over 50 m² is sold, rented out or undergoes major renovation.  

• Main contents  
  – Energy class (A–G), sometimes expressed as “epc_egienergiklass.” The latest class is the one that applies.  
  – Total annual energy use, typically given in kWh/m² and broken down by heating, hot water, ventilation, etc.  
  – Heated floor area (Atemp), recorded under “epc_egenatemp.”  
  – Building type and structure (e.g. detached house, apartment block), recorded under “epc_egenbyggnadstyp.”  
  – Number of floors (“epc_egenantalplan”)

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any modification, upgrade or operational change that reduces the amount of energy needed to provide the same level of service—whether that’s heating, cooling, lighting or running equipment—without sacrificing comfort or productivity. In the context of buildings it typically involves measures such as:  
• Upgrading insulation in walls, roofs and floors to reduce heat loss or gain  
• Installing high-performance windows and doors with better thermal seals  
• Replacing old heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems with modern, high-efficiency models  
• Switching to LED or other low-energy lighting systems  
• Adding smart building controls (programmable thermostats, motion-sensing lighting, building-automation systems)  
• Sealing air leaks around ducts, pipes and openings  
• Selecting energy-efficient appliances and office equipment

• Lower energy use and operating cost

  – Reduced heating/cooling loads if designed to support night-time cooling  
  – Fewer CO₂ emissions over the building’s lifetime

  – Simpler installation (no large fans, motors or duct networks)  
  – Minimal moving parts → lower risk of breakdowns  
  – No regular fan repairs and fewer filter replacements

  – Continues to function during power outages or mechanical failures  
  – Less dependence on complex controls and building-management systems

In the electric-vehicle industry the distinction between “normal” charging and “fast” charging generally comes down to both the type of current (AC vs. DC) and the power level:

1. Normal (AC) charging  
   • Power: typically from about 3 kW up to 22 kW  
   • Connection: the car’s onboard charger converts AC to DC internally  
   • Use case: home charging overnight, workplace charging

2. Fast charging  
   a. Fast AC charging  
      – Power: roughly 22 kW to 43 kW AC  
      – Less common (requires heavier wiring and a more capable onboard charger)  
   b. Fast DC charging  
      – Power: typically starts at around 50 kW DC and can go up to 150 kW or more  
      – The charger delivers DC directly to the battery, bypassing the onboard charger  

Key boundary:  
– For most drivers and public-charging networks, anything above 22 kW is considered “fast” charging.  
– In practice you will see DC fast-chargers rated from 50 kW up to 350 kW (so-called ultra-fast or high-power charging).

In Sweden (and in most European countries following EN 12464-1), stairwells are classified as circulation areas where safety is paramount. The recommended lighting levels are as follows:

1. Normal (operational) lighting  
   • Maintained horizontal illuminance: min. 100 lux averaged on the walking surface (typically measured about 0.2 m above each step)  
   • Uniformity (Uo = Emin/Emean): ≥ 0.4  

   This level ensures good visibility of risers and treads and helps prevent trips and falls.

2. Emergency lighting  
   • Minimum maintained horizontal illuminance: 1 lux on the walking surface  
   • This level applies if the normal supply fails; it must come from an independent emergency power source and cover the entire escape route.

By adhering to these values, you ensure compliance with both safety regulations and user comfort in stairwells.

Improving lighting in basement areas is often a matter of combining daylight-harvesting strategies, efficient artificial fixtures and good lighting design. Below are several approaches you can adopt:

1. Bring in Natural Light Where Possible  
   • Light wells or window wells: install or enlarge small windows at ground level and line the well walls with reflective material to bounce daylight in.  
   • Tubular daylight devices (sun tunnels): channel sunlight from the roof into the basement via highly reflective tubing and a clear dome.  
   • Skylights or light shafts: if the basement is directly below a roof-accessible space, consider installing a skylight with a light shaft down to the basement ceiling.

2. Select Efficient, High-Quality Fixtures  
   • LED panels and downlights: choose dimmable, high-lumen, low-profile LED fixtures for uniform ceiling illumination.  
   • High CRI (>80): ensures colors look natural and the space feels more welcoming.

In Sweden, stairwells are regarded as “unheated service spaces” in Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR). The key points are:

• Minimum temperature  
  – To avoid frost damage, moisture problems and ice on steps, the indoor air must not drop below about 12 °C.  
  
• Recommended operating range  
  – For reasonable comfort when people pass through, designers and property managers often aim for 15–18 °C.  
  
• Energy implications  
  – Heating a large stairwell to living-room temperatures (20 °C and above) is seldom energy-efficient. Keeping it at 12–18 °C balances user safety and comfort with reasonable energy use.

There is no separate EPC parameter for stairwell temperature, but the building’s overall energy class (epc_egienergiklass) will reflect how efficiently common areas such as stairwells are heated.
